This would only work if there is an equal amount of cytochrome c present. However, there is one to two orders of magnitude more quinone than cytochrome c so where do the electrons come from that reduce the Q-pool?

2) Evolution did not act at the level of individual chromatophores but on the survival fitness of the intact organism.

3) The authors use efficiency values without specifying exactly what they mean. I presume that they have had a certain numerical value for "delta-Gp" in mind (i.e. the standard free energy of hydrolysis of ATP), and then calculate efficiency as the ratio of the caloric value of the photons over the free energy of the corresponding ATP hydrolysis. This should however be made explicit. Furthermore, they now and then shift back and forth from oxygenic to anoxygenic photosynthesis (e.g. Discussion, first paragraph), which is not proper because in oxygenic photosynthesis the majority of the energy conservation goes into redox energy (i.e. NADPH). Estimates that anoxygenic photosynthesis has a free-energy efficiency in the order of 10% have already been available for a long time (Hellingwerf, K. J., Crielaard, W., & Westerhoff, H. V. (1993). Comparison of retinal-based and chlorophyll-based photosynthesis: A biothermokinetic description of photochemical reaction centers. Modern trends in biothermokinetics (pp. 45-52) Springer).

4) Beyond the LH/RC itself, nowhere in the modelling has any leak-reaction taken into account. Two examples that would have been very relevant to take into account are: (a) the short-cut in electron transfer in the cytochrome bc1 complex that may occur if the second electron of quinol is also directly transferred to the Rieske protein and (b) passive proton leakage through the chromatophore membrane (which may be very much dependent of the protein composition of the vesicles, due to curvature effects). Related to this is the fact that the authors seem to suggest that proton transport merely leads to a pH change (see discussion on acidification), whereas presumably the energetic coupling between the proton pumping system and the ATP synthase is through a transmembrane electrical potential gradient.

5) What precisely does the atomistic description of the light harvesting and trapping process contribute to the calculation of the efficiency? Could the energy transfer and trapping process not be captured by a single effective rate constant that is a function of the fraction of open and closed traps and the ratio of LH2 to RC-LH1. See many earlier papers on the subject: Vredenberg and Duysens, Duysens CIBA foundation, Den Hollander et al., Trissl et al., Joliot cs etc.

Reviewer #2:

The manuscript by Sener and co-workers presents a model of a Rhodobacter sphaeroides chromatophore. The model describes how the illumination of a chromatophore suspension results in ATP production. The ultimate goal of the modeling is to understand how the ATP yield is coupled with the intensity of light. The main virtue of the model is that it couples the quantum physics of light absorption/procession with the chemistry of ATP synthesis. The model gives reasonable values of ATP yield in response to low light, which is physiological for these bacteria. Development of such a global model, which covers events over a time span of 14 orders of magnitude, required certain simplifications, which is understandable. Unfortunately, from the opinion of this reviewer, the simplifications preclude from making physiologically relevant conclusions from the modeling, at least, at the given stage.

Still the model itself is a great achievement and the manuscript deserves publication albeit after certain amendments.

1) Since the physiological relevance of the results obtained is questionable, the main result of this study seems to be the model itself. Therefore, the description of the model should be moved from the Materials and methods into the Results. Otherwise the manuscript is incomprehensive, taking into account that the format of eLife implies Materials and methods after Results. The Materials and methods section should then contain only technical/purely methodical points; supplementary materials, at least partly, could be also moved into Materials and methods.

2) The current simplified model lacks two important modules, which, hopefully, would be added in the future. These are the protonmotive force and reversible NADH dehydrogenase. The authors admit the absence of these modules, but did not consider the consequences of their absence in full extent. This should be done in the Discussion.

3) In the absence of these two modules, the authors conclude that "energy conversion in the chromatophore appears to be rate-limited primarily by cytbc1" and that "cytbc1-limited kinetics prevents an overproduction of protons at sustained high-light conditions,…thereby protecting the chromatophore against overacidification of its interior and assuring vesicle integrity at high-light conditions".

In real phototropic bacteria, the situation is more complex. Obviously, the function of a photosynthetic apparatus, such as bacterial chromatophore or a chloroplast thylakoid, is to produce ATP and NAD(P)H. In thylakoids, NAD(P)H molecules are produced via direct reduction of NAD(P)+ by the Photosystem I. In Rb. sphaerides, the redox potential of the RC is too high for NAD(P)H generation. Therefore, NAD(P)H is produced via reversing the NAD(P)H dehydrogenase. The reversion requires (1) high protonmotive force and (2) reduced ubiquinol pool. Therefore, the overreduction of the ubiquinol pool in Rb. sphaeroides is a precondition for the NAD(P)H production; it should increase the overall efficiency of the system. Furthermore, the overacidification of the interior is prevented not by the overreduction of the ubiquinone pool, but by the high sensitivity of the cytbc1 to the membrane potential. High voltage, needed to drive the NAD(P)+ reduction (see above), slows the turnover of the cytbc1 dramatically, essentially blocking its turnover at voltages above 150 mV. Hence at high, physiological values of protonmotive force the turnover of the cytbc1 is essentially limited by the proton discharge, specifically via the ATP synthase and the reverse NAD(P)H dehydrogenase. The operation of the cytbc1 close to equilibrium additionally increases the efficiency of energy conversion.

The reviewer admits that the data on synthesis of NAD(P)H in Rb. sphaeroides are too scarce to be used for verification of the model. The authors, accordingly, have tested their model by using more abundant data that were obtained with chromatophore suspensions in the absence of NAD(P)+, in experiments where the function of the RC, cytbc1 and/or ATP synthase were studied. And still, the discussion of physiological consequences from the given model should be truncated dramatically as misleading. The physiology could be discussed in further publications, after the membrane potential and NAD(P)H synthesis would be explicitly included in the model.

Instead, the Discussion section should include comparison of the given model with the earlier models of chromatophore systems (e.g. from the group of Helms) and the approaches used.

Reviewer #3:

The authors present an important theoretical investigation of the performance and limitations of the photosynthetic chromatophore complex of purple bacteria. This light-harvesting system is of great interest as a model system that contains numerous characteristic properties inherent to all natural light-harvesting systems. This work is a continuation of a long line of first-rate papers published by the authors on this topic, is extremely well written, and merits publication in its current form.

There appears to be a minor inconsistency in the units of intensity employed. In the second paragraph of section 4.2 the authors define light intensity, I, in units of [photons absorbed per second], whereas light intensity is often defined in units of [photons absorbed per meter squared per second]. As defined, this intensity is in fact a power, which is also called a 'radiant flux' in radiometry. This in contrast with the more conventional definition of intensity, in the caption of Figure 2, where units of [Watts per meter squared] are used. Clarification of these different definitions would be useful.

In the third paragraph of section 4.2, the authors switch to defining 'I' as 'illumination,' which may further confuse the reader. Ideally 'radiant flux' or 'absorbed light power' or similar terminology would be employed throughout, or alternatively 'illumination' would be defined.

The explanation provided in the fourth and fifth paragraphs of section 2.2 for the suboptimal (nB, nRC) values in low-light adapted vesicles is appealing, but it does not appear to be supported by calculations. Despite the fact that the model only applies in steady-state, is it possible to perform a simple simulation to support this interpretation, even qualitatively?

The choice of initial condition assumed in Equation 9 may possibly be over-simplifying because each complex (LH2, LH1 and RC) does not necessarily have the same absorption spectrum, since at a given wavelength, the probability of absorption of a photon is not the same for each complex. In this scenario, the initial condition should then be wavelength dependent. While the authors state that the quantum yield is not strongly dependent on the choice of P(0), a specific example to demonstrate this would be helpful.

[Editors' note: further revisions were requested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Overall energy conversion efficiency of a photosynthetic vesicle" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Michael Marletta (Senior editor), a Reviewing editor, and two reviewers.

On the basis of the referee reports on the revised manuscript, only relatively minor additional changes are required. Reviewer #2 is concerned that some issues have not been fully addressed in the revision. In the following I list the main points.

1) The reviewer maintains that "the model does not consider the production of NADH at all." Therefore, "no statements on the energy conversion efficiency could be done with the current model." The reviewer is concerned that the issue of NADH production and its impact on the model and its assessment are not discussed adequately, and advises "to read the primary literature on the mechanism of NADH production and provide references to this literature (currently they refer only to the paper of Klamt et al. where bacterial photosynthesis was modeled by using several dozen parameters that were more or less freely variable). The primary literature describes how the NADH-dehydrogenase makes NADH by driving the reverse (uphill) electron transfer from the ubiquinone pool to NAD+ with the help of membrane potential. This mechanism differs from the NAD(P)H production in green plants where NAD(P)+ is directly reduced by photoexcitated electrons in a reaction that is independent of membrane potential. The dependence of the light-driven NADH production on membrane potential, specific for Rhodobacter and other purple phototrophic bacteria, should have shaped the properties of their energy-converting machinery."

Recommended action: Whereas I do not see the lack of NADH production as a fundamental flaw in the model (after all, all models are incomplete), this point should be made clearer to the reader. Conclusions drawn from the model should be qualified accordingly. In particular, in the discussion of the energy conversion efficiency, relevant limitations of the model should be stated.

2) The reviewer also asks to point out clearly that "the experimental data that were used for testing the model were not obtained with chromatophores in vivo," but for "an artificial system – a suspension of chromatophores in a pH-buffer, in the presence of electron donors and redox mediators, but in the absence of physiological compounds such as NAD+/NADH (a Dutton/Crofts system)."

Recommended action: Point out the distinction between the in-vitro experiments and the more complex in-vivo situation.

3) The reviewer also argues that the effect of a transmembrane proton gradient, which is not included explicitly in the model, should be discussed. The reviewer emphasizes that the issue is not "proton migration from the bc1 complex to ATP synthase" but protonmotive force.

Recommended action: Discuss the issue of protonmotive force. Examine which conclusions would likely be impacted by the explicit treatment of PMF in the model, and qualify them accordingly. If none of the conclusions would be affected, state that the model is robust with respect to the neglect of explicit modeling of PMF.

4) The reviewer suggests adding a description of the model to the Results section.

results.result: The chromatophore of purple bacteria (specifically Rhodobacter sphaeroides) is characterized as an intracellular spherical vesicle of 50-70 nm diameter, formed through invagination of the intracytoplasmic membrane, comprising over a hundred protein complexes (primarily LH2, RC-LH1, cytbc1, and ATP synthases), 16,000 lipids, and ~900 quinone/quinol molecules, totaling ~100 million atoms including solvent. The chromatophore exists in numerous copies per cell and operates typically under low light conditions to efficiently convert sunlight into ATP.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C14-C18, C24, C61, and C67 collectively describe the structural and functional characteristics of the chromatophore based on prior experimental work (AFM, EM, crystallography, mass spectroscopy, proteomics) cited throughout. The structural model is well-documented with specific quantitative details (size, composition, stoichiometry) and validated through a 100 ns MD simulation (C68). These are primarily descriptive claims about the system under study, well-supported by cited literature and the authors' prior modeling work.

results.result: The study identifies quinol turnover at cytochrome bc1 complex as the rate-limiting step in chromatophore energy conversion, with the quinone/quinol pool of ~900 molecules acting in a quasi-stationary state. The quantum yield (~0.91) does not constitute a limiting factor for overall energy conversion efficiency because excitation transfer and charge separation (rates ~(10 ps)⁻¹) occur much faster than internal conversion and fluorescence losses (rates ~(1 ns)⁻¹). The quinone/quinol pool redox state adapts to light changes on a ~0.5 s timescale.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 state key modeling assumptions that are justified through comparison of turnover capacities at different components (detailed in Materials and Methods). The identification of cytbc1 as rate-limiting is supported by quantitative comparison showing cytbc1 turnover capacity (160 s⁻¹) is exceeded by RC quinol production capacity (846 s⁻¹) at just 5% sunlight. The high quantum yield (C29, C84) is explained mechanistically by the timescale separation between productive and loss processes. The quasi-stationary assumption (C5) and adaptation timescale (C85) are supported by cited experimental work.

results.result: At light intensities equivalent to 1% and 3% of full sunlight, the chromatophore vesicle produces ATP at rates of 82 s⁻¹ and 118 s⁻¹, respectively, representing 79% and 51% of the maximum possible rates among all stoichiometries. At the high-light limit, ATP synthesis approaches 158 s⁻¹. These rates are consistent with experimental observations of 0.017-0.05 ATP molecules per BChl per second (corresponding to ~43-130 ATP s⁻¹ for the modeled vesicle).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C30-C32, C63-C64 present the primary quantitative results for ATP production rates calculated from the kinetic model (Equations 11-20). The calculated rates show reasonable agreement with experimental measurements from two independent studies (Saphon et al., 1975; Clark et al., 1983), providing validation. The model predictions fall within the experimental range, though the comparison involves some uncertainty as one experimental value was from a different species (Rhodopseudomonas capsulata). The consistency between model and experiment supports the validity of the rate-limiting assumptions.

results.result: The energy conversion efficiency of ATP synthesis at illuminations corresponding to 1%-5% of full sunlight is calculated to be 12%-4%, respectively. The efficiency computed for the chromatophore model ranges between 0%-17% across all light intensities. These values are below the previously estimated upper limit of 30% for photosynthesis in Rba. sphaeroides.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C33-C35 present calculated energy conversion efficiencies based on Equation 21, which compares ATP synthesis energy to absorbed photon energy. The efficiency values are internally consistent with the ATP production rates (C6, C30-C31) and show the expected decrease with increasing light intensity due to saturation effects. The comparison with the 30% upper limit estimate (C34) provides context, though this prior estimate may have different assumptions. The efficiency calculation depends on the assumed ATP hydrolysis energy and number of c-subunits in ATP synthase (acknowledged as uncertain in Discussion), but the relative trends are robust.

results.result: The vesicle stoichiometry is evolutionarily adapted to low light intensities but is suboptimal for steady-state ATP turnover. The native cytbc1:RC ratio of 1:3 could be improved for ATP production, but the observed composition provides protection against over-illumination by limiting proton gradient generation and preventing overacidification. The chromatophore is a specialized device that performs robustly at low light intensity while featuring protective measures that dissipate energy at higher intensities, with robustness against damage superseding optimality under idealized steady-state conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C47-C48, C58-C60 present the key biological interpretation of the modeling results. The suboptimality for steady-state ATP production is demonstrated quantitatively in Figure 3, showing the native composition achieves only 79% (1% sunlight) or 51% (3% sunlight) of maximum possible rates. The protective function interpretation is well-reasoned: the low cytbc1 count limits proton turnover to below ATP synthase capacity, preventing overacidification during sustained high illumination. This trade-off between optimality and robustness is a biologically plausible evolutionary strategy, though direct experimental evidence for the protective mechanism is not provided. The interpretation is consistent with the quantitative results but represents an inference about evolutionary adaptation.

results.result: The efficiency curve determined for the purple bacterial chromatophore indicates specialization for low-light intensities.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 summarizes the interpretation of Figure 2B, which shows efficiency declining from ~12% at 1% sunlight to <0.1% beyond full sunlight. This pattern is consistent with the known ecology of purple bacteria (low-light habitats) and follows logically from the rate-limiting behavior of cytbc1. The specialization interpretation is well-supported by both the quantitative results and biological context.

results.result: Chromatophore vesicles typically contain 1-2 ATP synthases, with proteomics suggesting preferential co-location with LH2 subunits. A single ATP synthase is sufficient to utilize the proton turnover of an entire chromatophore. Vesicles occasionally fuse through membrane tubes, permitting proton sharing between neighboring chromatophores and reducing the need for redundant ATP synthases.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52, C70-C71 describe ATP synthase stoichiometry and organization based on cited experimental work. The sufficiency of a single ATP synthase (C51) is supported by comparison of turnover capacities: ATP synthase capacity (2160 s⁻¹ for 2 synthases) exceeds cytbc1 capacity (640 s⁻¹), so one synthase would be adequate. The vesicle fusion observation (C52) provides an interesting biological context for the low ATP synthase count. These claims are well-supported by cited literature and quantitative analysis.

results.result: Background claims about photosynthetic organisms, purple bacteria, and prior work on photosynthetic optimization and robustness, including the use of Förster mechanism and quantum coherence for excitation transfer, the evolutionary age and relative simplicity of purple bacterial systems, the role of open/closed RCs in efficiency, and prior demonstrations of robustness in pigment networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13, C19-C21, C26-C27, C43, C45-C46, C76 are background statements about prior work, all supported by appropriate citations. These provide context for the current study but do not represent new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the statements are consistent with the photosynthesis literature.

results.result: The chromatophore model is based on integration of AFM, EM, crystallography, mass spectroscopy, proteomics, and optical spectroscopy data, and has been validated through a 100 ns MD simulation to test model viability.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C68 describe the model construction and validation methodology. The multi-technique integration approach is well-documented in the cited work (Cartron et al., 2014) and represents state-of-the-art structural modeling. The 100 ns MD simulation provides computational validation of the structural model's stability, though this timescale is short relative to the millisecond processes being modeled kinetically.

results.result: The quinone/quinol pool and proton gradient function as energy buffers between light harvesting and ATP synthesis stages. The chromatophore utilizes the proton motive force for NADH production via NADH dehydrogenase, thereby controlling the quinone/quinol pool redox state.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 describe the energy buffering function and the role of NADH dehydrogenase in redox control, both supported by cited work (Klamt et al., 2008). These are established aspects of chromatophore function that provide context for the modeling approach, though NADH dehydrogenase is not explicitly included in the structural model.

results.result: Efficient energy conversion requires robustness with respect to supramolecular organization since chromatophores are heterogeneous. The quantum yield is solely a function of pigment network geometry, independent of light intensity, and is close to unity (~0.91) for chlorophyll absorption. Carotenoids transfer excitation within <1 ps to nearby BChls and quench triplet states. Exciton-based excitation transfer proceeds within 10-100 ps, with BChls rapidly forming thermally equilibrated exciton states within ~1 ps.
results.evaluation: Claims C75, C77-C83 describe the quantum mechanical aspects of light harvesting and excitation transfer, all well-supported by the authors' prior computational work and cited experimental studies. The quantum yield calculation (q=0.91) is based on established generalized Förster theory (Equations 2-10) with parameters validated against experimental timescales. The timescale hierarchy (ps for transfer vs ns for losses) is well-established experimentally and computationally.

results.result: The present study differs from earlier chromatophore modeling by using an explicit atomic-detail structural model and few experimentally determined rate constants rather than many adjustable parameters. A steady-state description is employed such that non-rate-limiting steps can be omitted. The primary conclusions would not be affected by more detailed description of individual proton translocation steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99, C102 describe the methodological approach and its advantages over prior work (Geyer et al., 2007, 2010). The use of an atomic-detail structural model and experimentally determined rate constants (rather than fitted parameters) is a clear strength. The steady-state assumption and focus on rate-limiting steps is justified for the timescales considered. The robustness claim (C102) is reasonable given that the rate-limiting step (cytbc1 turnover) is well-established experimentally, though more detailed modeling could reveal additional complexity.

results.result: Integrative models of organelle function provide a bridge between experimental methods lacking temporal/spatial detail and microscopic simulations spanning multiple scales relevant for cellular function.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is a general statement about the value of integrative modeling approaches, which is well-illustrated by the present study. The chromatophore model successfully bridges atomic-detail structure with millisecond-scale function, demonstrating the utility of multi-scale modeling. This is a reasonable perspective statement supported by the work presented.
